module_title: Trial in Absentia, Bail Overhaul, and Mercy Petitions
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and Judiciary Mains, this level explores the most radical systemic shifts: holding trials without the accused, the drastic changes to undertrial bail, and strict new timelines for criminal justice delivery.

core_concepts.title: Trial in Absentia (Section 356 BNSS)
core_concepts.description:
A paradigm shift in Indian criminal jurisprudence.
- CrPC Rule: A trial could generally not proceed if the accused absconded. The trial would stall indefinitely.
- BNSS Rule: If an accused is declared a 'Proclaimed Offender' and evades trial for **90 days**, the court can proceed with the trial, record evidence, and even pronounce a conviction/sentence in their absence. 
- Safeguard: The accused can appeal the conviction if they surrender within 30 days and prove they had no notice of the trial.

core_concepts.title: Bail for Undertrial Prisoners (Section 479 BNSS)
core_concepts.description:
Replaces Section 436A of CrPC to massively reduce prison overcrowding.
- First-Time Offenders: Must be released on bail if they have undergone **one-third (1/3rd)** of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for the offense (it was one-half under CrPC).
- Multiple Offenses Exception: A massive restriction. Section 479 does NOT apply to undertrials involved in 'more than one offense' or those facing life imprisonment. (Critics note that police often stack multiple charges/FIRs against an accused, nullifying this benefit).

core_concepts.title: Mercy Petitions (Section 472 BNSS)
core_concepts.description:
Codifies and restricts the process of seeking pardon from the President (Art 72) / Governor (Art 161).
- Time Limit: A mercy petition must be filed within **60 days** after the Supreme Court dismisses the appeal/review.
- Locus Standi: The petition can ONLY be filed by the convict or their legal heir. NGOs, civil society groups, or random citizens can no longer file mercy petitions on behalf of death-row convicts.

core_concepts.title: Strict Timelines for Justice Delivery
core_concepts.description:
BNSS introduces strict statutory timelines to cure judicial delays:
- Framing of Charges: Must be done within **60 days** of the first hearing on the charge.
- Pronouncement of Judgment: Judgment must be delivered within **30 days** (extendable to 45 days) after the trial concludes.
- Medical Reports: Rape examination reports must be forwarded to the investigating officer within **7 days**.

important_entities.name: Directorate of Prosecution (Section 26 BNSS)
important_entities.key_fact: Mandatory setup at State and District levels.
important_entities.significance: BNSS strengthens the separation of the investigating agency (Police) and the prosecuting agency (Lawyers). It makes the Directorate of Prosecution mandatory, ensuring that decisions to prosecute or withdraw cases are made with legal rigor, independent of police pressure.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The 'Trial in Absentia for All' Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Trial in absentia under Section 356 does NOT apply to every missing accused. It strictly applies only to a person who has officially been declared a **'Proclaimed Offender'** (which requires a specific judicial order under Section 84 BNSS for serious crimes).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: For first-time undertrial offenders, the threshold to claim mandatory bail dropped from serving 50% of the max sentence to serving 33.3% of it.

exam_strategy_tips: If an exam asks 'What is the new statutory deadline for a judge to pronounce a judgment after the trial ends under BNSS?', select **30 days**.
